title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency
authors: Ilya V. Chepkasov, Alexander V. Shapeev, Alexander G. Kvashnin
abstract: Developing a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) that is accurate for the specific conditions under which it will be applied, rather than simply for the predefined configurations chosen by the model developer, is a significant challenge in atomistic simulation. Active learning (AL) addresses this challenge by closing the loop between candidate generation, data selection, reference calculation, and model updating. Here, we survey more than seventy studies, with an emphasis on work from 2020 to 2026, to understand how active learning has evolved from a niche, on-the-fly training technique for query-by-committee and Gaussian process force fields into a diverse family of data-efficient strategies. he reviewed examples include on-the-fly molecular dynamics, active data selection for fine-tuning pretrained models, kernel- and representation-based acquisition using frozen pretrained models, and reaction-aware sampling for chemical systems far from equilibrium. We explore the use of active learning in elemental and alloy mechanics, hydrogen and ion diffusion, ferroelectrics and effective Hamiltonians of functional materials, reactive and photochemical dynamics, high-entropy and compositionally disordered materials, as well as generative and autonomous material discovery pipelines. Drawing on a growing body of critical, methodologically self-aware literature, we also show that this achievement carries systematic caveats. Uncertainty estimates are not interchangeable across model architectures and are frequently the least reliable exactly where they matter most. We close by discussing the outlook for standardized, uncertainty-calibrated, and observable-targeted active-learning workflows in the foundation-model era.

infographic.key_insight: Active learning makes machine-learning interatomic potentials more data-efficient by selecting reference calculations relevant to their intended simulation conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive training can support atomistic modeling of mechanics, diffusion, functional materials, and reactive systems while targeting costly reference calculations where needed.
method: Generate candidate atomic configurations and select informative samples.
Run reference calculations, update the potential, and repeat.
Use uncertainty-, representation-, or reaction-aware selection, including workflows with pretrained models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The review surveys more than 70 studies, emphasizing 2020–2026, across diverse materials and simulation tasks rather than reporting a single benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Uncertainty estimates differ across model architectures and can be least reliable in the unfamiliar regimes where trustworthy selection matters most.
infographic.paper_title: Active Learning for Interatomic Potentials: A Review of Uncertainty-Driven Data Efficiency

title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations
authors: Benran Zhang, Byeongchan Lee, Zien Zhu, Chih-En Hsu, Zhenfa Zheng, Hung-Chung Hsueh
abstract: Many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) methods, including the GW approximation, the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) method, and GW perturbation theory (GWPT), among others, provide accurate first-principles descriptions of excited-state properties and multiparticle interactions of materials. However, their use remains limited due to complex multi-software workflows, interdependent physical parameters, and substantial theoretical expertise. Large language model (LLM) agents, which couple a language model to software tools, show potential in automating computational tasks, but MBPT remains an unaddressed challenge. We show that LLM agents tested in our work, including frontier models such as Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, do not reliably construct MBPT workflows in one attempt, suggesting that correct setup requires expert knowledge and consistency that current models lack. Across tested model-harness combinations, out-of-the-box agents average 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow benchmarks, with strong model dependence and large run-to-run variation. Errors typically originate from cross-stage inconsistencies that surface only several stages after they are introduced. We therefore develop AI-Donkey, an agentic framework that combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to enable high-fidelity GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT calculations and analyses. With AI-Donkey, all tested agents, from frontier proprietary models to open-weight models, produce complete, runnable MBPT workflows with no observed run-to-run variation. We further demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing on 1D, 2D, and bulk materials, including the many-body enhancement of Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling in polar semiconductors. Our approach provides a general framework for knowledge engineering to enable reliable agentic workflows in computational materials science.

infographic.key_insight: AI-Donkey combines expert-curated knowledge with deterministic execution to make LLM-driven many-body perturbation theory workflows reliable in the reported tests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could reduce specialist setup effort for calculating excited-state properties and particle interactions across 1D, 2D, and bulk materials.
method: Benchmark unassisted LLM agents on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT workflow construction.
Integrate expert-curated knowledge and deterministic execution through AI-Donkey.
Demonstrate autonomous calculations and post-processing, including many-body enhancement of Fröhlich electron-phonon coupling.
infographic.evidence_signal: Out-of-the-box agents averaged 54%, 36%, and 19% on GW, GW-BSE, and GWPT benchmarks, respectively; with AI-Donkey, all tested agents produced complete, runnable workflows with no observed run-to-run variation.
infographic.watch_item: Runnable workflows do not alone establish physical accuracy or convergence; reliability beyond the tested cases and curated knowledge remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Enabling large language model agents for high-fidelity many-body perturbation theory calculations

title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential
authors: Nils-Ruben Skogemyr, Albin Sjöstedt, Isak Wernroth, Isak Häggqvist, Isac Ljungwald, Hans-Ove Åkesson
abstract: Defect engineering is a crucial tool for tuning and tailoring the properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials. A key challenge is identifying which defects are kinetically stable at room temperature and sufficiently promising to warrant further investigation. However, identifying stable defects with suitable properties using first-principles calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT) is computationally demanding, effectively limiting the scope of high-throughput studies. In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. A total of 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database are simulated using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) at both 0 K and 300 K. The results show that MACE successfully reproduces the overall sorption trends observed in DFT calculations at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost. Simulations performed at 300 K further indicate that the qualitative sorption trends remain largely the same when including finite-temperature effects. These findings demonstrate that MACE-driven MD can be used as an effective high-throughput prescreening tool for defect-related studies in 2D materials, specially related to sorption. While conventional first-principles methods, such as DFT, remain necessary for accurate and quantitative validation, the use of MLIPs enables MD simulations of finite-temperature defect behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of DFT-based MD.

infographic.key_insight: MACE-driven molecular dynamics reproduces overall DFT sorption trends for defects in 2D materials, with qualitative trends largely unchanged at 300 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Low-cost ML-driven simulations enable high-throughput prescreening of defect sorption behavior before expensive first-principles validation.
method: Evaluate 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database.
Use the MACE machine learning interatomic potential for simulations at 0 K and 300 K.
Compare adsorption-versus-absorption trends with prior high-throughput DFT results.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 17,624 structures, MACE reproduced overall DFT sorption trends at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost, while 300 K simulations retained largely similar qualitative trends.
infographic.watch_item: Agreement in aggregate sorption trends does not establish quantitative accuracy or long-term defect stability; DFT validation remains necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential

title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Response Tensors in Crystalline Magnets: Application to Kagome Metals
authors: Yu-Hsuan Lin, Joel E. Moore
abstract: The prediction of response tensors from magnetic textures is a crucial challenge in the study of noncollinear magnets. Existing methods for constructing descriptors of a given response tensor are limited to first-order multipole expansions or restricted to simple magnetic structures. In this work, we construct a complete symmetry-invariant descriptor basis for arbitrary crystal structures and magnetic textures, providing interpretable features for machine learning modeling of response tensors. We modify the standard principal component analysis framework and derive uncorrelated order parameters that are hierarchically stable: extending the order parameter space to include higher-degree spin order introduces additional order parameters that are uncorrelated to the previous ones. We apply this framework to regression and classification of the anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) in a magnetic kagome lattice. In particular, in the regime where AHC is well modeled by linear regression of the symmetry-invariant order parameters, we find that the squared regression coefficients, ranked by their magnitude, obey a Zipf-like power law: $β_{r}^2 \propto r^{-α}$. Our method provides a systematic route to construct interpretable order parameters of all spin orders that connect the symmetry of a magnetic crystal to its response tensors.

infographic.key_insight: A complete symmetry-invariant descriptor basis connects magnetic textures to response tensors through interpretable, hierarchically stable order parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a systematic way to build physics-informed machine-learning models of response tensors in crystalline magnets.
method: Construct symmetry-invariant descriptors for arbitrary crystal structures and magnetic textures.
Modify principal component analysis to obtain uncorrelated order parameters that remain stable as higher spin orders are added.
Use the order parameters to regress and classify anomalous Hall conductivity in a magnetic kagome lattice.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the regime where linear regression models anomalous Hall conductivity well, ranked squared regression coefficients follow a Zipf-like power law; the abstract reports no numerical accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is demonstrated on a magnetic kagome lattice, so predictive performance and computational cost for other crystal structures remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Response Tensors in Crystalline Magnets: Application to Kagome Metals

title: Oxygen on Rh(100) revisited with ultra-high precision
authors: Lutz Hammer, Tilman Kißlinger, Margareta Wagner, Reinhard B. Neder, Michael Schmid, Ulrike Diebold
abstract: We have reanalyzed the 0.25 and 0.50 monolayer (ML) phases of oxygen on the catalytically important Rh(100) surface by quantitative low-energy electron diffraction (LEED), variable-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and density functional theory (DFT). For both phases, the crystallographic structure could be determined by LEED structure analyses with single-digit picometer precision enabled by ultra-low Pendry R factors of R$_\mathrm{P}$ $\approx$ 0.07. For the (2$\times$2)-O phase at 0.25 ML we find oxygen adsorbed at fourfold hollow sites in accordance to earlier results [Surf. Sci. 207 (1988) 55], however, with a pronounced buckling within the second layer of the otherwise unreconstructed substrate. For the 0.50 monolayer phase, we recently identified a (2$\sqrt{2}$ $\times$ 2$\sqrt{2}$)R45$^\circ$-4O ground state structure [Phys. Rev. Res. 8 (2026) 023296], which decomposes into a large number of nano-domains already at temperatures below 100 K. In this paper we provide a detailed analysis of the atomic structure and the ordering behavior of this phase and resolve long-standing discrepancies with the original (2$\times$2)pg model [Phys. Rev. Lett. 82 (1999) 4874]. We further prove by short-range order simulations that the coherent superposition of scattering contributions of the nano-domains leads to a virtual extinction of diffraction spots, which has concealed the true periodicity and symmetry of this phase for so long.

infographic.key_insight: Ultra-high-precision analysis reveals subsurface buckling beneath 0.25 ML oxygen on Rh(100) and explains how nanoscale domains conceal the true periodicity of the 0.50 ML phase.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate oxygen–rhodium surface structures provide a stronger foundation for atomistic models of this catalytically important material.
method: Quantitative low-energy electron diffraction (LEED) structure analysis
Variable-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and density functional theory (DFT)
Short-range-order simulations of coherent scattering from nanoscale domains
infographic.evidence_signal: LEED analyses achieved single-digit-picometer structural precision with Pendry R factors near 0.07 for both coverages, while simulations reproduced the near-extinction of diffraction spots.
infographic.watch_item: The 0.50 ML ground-state structure fragments into nanoscale domains even below 100 K, complicating diffraction-based identification of its periodicity and symmetry.
infographic.paper_title: Oxygen on Rh(100) revisited with ultra-high precision

title: Interplay between high-entropy effects and the superionic transition in fluorite oxides: A liquid-like perspective
authors: Fengnian Zhuang, Gaosheng Yan, Hong Chen, Yi Zhang, Wenshan Yu, Minglong Xu
abstract: Minor actinide (MA)-bearing mixed oxide (MOX), a prominent high-entropy ceramic (HEC), is a promising candidate for advanced fast reactor fuels. Using a hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics (MC/MD) approach, we reveal that Np and Am segregation establishes a distinct short-range order (SRO) that induces severe lattice distortion. We uncover a competitive mechanism between localized high-entropy blocking effects and collective superionic dynamics, where the anionic kinetic and structural evolution within the 2000-2800 K range is partitioned and governed by the Tammann crossover temperature and superionic transition temperature. In the low-temperature regime, severe lattice distortions induced by the SRO structures create localized electrostatic and strain-coupled potential wells, which spatially confine the O-ions and lead to their sluggish diffusion. The system exhibits increased dynamical heterogeneity as thermal activation alleviates these structural constraints. Crucially, these localized traps spontaneously transform into a highly interconnected, string-like polyhedral topological network. Driven by the maximization of configurational entropy, this structural change creates low-viscosity transport pathways that trigger confinement-enhanced diffusion. Consequently, a dramatic kinetic inversion occurs, where the O-ion mobility of SRO model surpasses that of random solid solution (RSS) model via an entropy-driven compensation mechanism. Finally, through Gibbs free energy minimization and defect analysis, structural and thermodynamic origins of the superionic transition in HEC are elucidated. This study unveils how local chemical ordering regulates ion transport under extreme conditions, providing theoretical support for the design of high-performance nuclear fuels with both superior radiation tolerance and optimized mass transfer capabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Short-range chemical order in high-entropy fluorite oxides initially traps oxygen ions but evolves into interconnected transport networks that enable mobility to exceed that of a random solid solution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling local chemical order could help optimize oxygen transport in minor-actinide-bearing mixed-oxide fuels for advanced fast reactors.
method: Hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations
Comparison of short-range-ordered and random solid-solution models
Gibbs free-energy minimization and defect analysis
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations across 2000–2800 K reveal a temperature-dependent mobility inversion linked to the evolution from localized oxygen traps to string-like polyhedral networks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulation-based findings without experimental validation, so applicability to irradiated reactor fuels remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Interplay between high-entropy effects and the superionic transition in fluorite oxides: A liquid-like perspective

title: OrderFlowDiT: Transport-Regularized Diffusion Transformer for Probabilistic Limit-Order Supply Forecasting
authors: Jung Hun Phee, Tucker Balch
abstract: We study the conditional distribution of limit-order volume submitted over the next five minutes, given the current order book and recent order flow. The task requires capturing price placement, total volume, and predictive uncertainty jointly. Coordinate-wise diffusion losses do not explicitly account for price displacement, while normalizing fields to unit mass removes information about total volume. Agreement on selected summary statistics also does not establish fidelity to the joint field distribution. We introduce OrderFlowDiT, a conditional Diffusion Transformer for unnormalized bid and ask volume-at-price fields, trained with an unbalanced optimal-transport (UOT) auxiliary loss. We also develop a full-field evaluation framework that combines a transport cost sensitive to price placement and total volume with proper scoring rules and calibration diagnostics. In the primary comparison on 1950 validation conditions across 30 U.S. equities, adding UOT reduces full-field transport cost by 45.8% and the transport energy score by 26.1% relative to training with mean squared error alone. Both measures improve for every stock. These findings support incorporating price geometry and volume into generative modeling, with field accuracy and predictive uncertainty evaluated together.

infographic.key_insight: Adding an unbalanced optimal-transport loss helps a Diffusion Transformer forecast limit-order volume distributions while preserving price placement and total volume.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This is financial-market forecasting research, not materials discovery, but its geometry-aware approach may inform engineering models of unnormalized spatial fields.
method: Condition on the current order book and recent order flow to forecast bid and ask volume-at-price fields over five minutes.
Train a conditional Diffusion Transformer with an auxiliary unbalanced optimal-transport loss.
Evaluate full-field fidelity and uncertainty using transport costs, proper scoring rules, and calibration diagnostics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1,950 validation conditions covering 30 U.S. equities, adding UOT reduced full-field transport cost by 45.8% and transport energy score by 26.1% versus MSE-only training, with both improving for every stock.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalization beyond the evaluated equities or applicability to materials-science datasets.
infographic.paper_title: OrderFlowDiT: Transport-Regularized Diffusion Transformer for Probabilistic Limit-Order Supply Forecasting

title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books
authors: Fernando Acero
abstract: Autoregressive transformers trained on limit order book (LOB) message streams are increasingly proposed as foundation models for market microstructure. Because the generative process of real markets is unknown, these models can be judged only by the realism of their output, leaving open what they actually learn. We make the question answerable by inverting the setup: we train GPT-style models on order flow from simulators whose latent parameters are known, so that the Bayes-optimal predictor, the generating state, and the exact data entropy serve as references. Measured against them, next-token pretraining on order flow implements amortized Bayesian inference over market regimes. The learned predictive matches the exact Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token and approaches the oracle floor even on a nonstationary family whose latent state drifts within an episode, a regime that requires filtering. The latent regime is linearly decodable from frozen activations, well above baselines, so a frozen-model read-out calibrates simulator parameters more accurately than windowed maximum likelihood at a fraction of the cost. In our experiments these capabilities are not produced by scale: capacity and token volume saturate early, and it is the diversity of training regimes, not the token count, that determines generalization to unseen markets. On real NASDAQ data, zero-shot transfer is set by how well the simulator prior covers real flow: an enriched mixture nearly closes the gap to an in-domain baseline, and pretraining beats from-scratch training at every budget across held-out tickers. Known ground truth turns average next-token loss, which is uninformative near the entropy floor, into an exact comparison against the Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors.

infographic.key_insight: Transformers trained on synthetic limit order book streams learn predictive behavior consistent with Bayesian inference over market regimes, with generalization driven more by regime diversity than scale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For financial simulation and model calibration—not materials discovery—frozen model representations enable accurate, lower-cost estimation of simulator parameters.
method: Train GPT-style models on synthetic order flow with known latent market parameters.
Compare predictions with exact Bayes-optimal predictors and oracle entropy floors, including drifting regimes.
Decode latent regimes from frozen activations and test transfer to real NASDAQ order flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports predictions within a millinat per token of the exact Bayes optimum, better calibration than windowed maximum likelihood, and pretraining gains at every tested budget across held-out tickers.
infographic.watch_item: Zero-shot transfer depends on how well the simulator prior covers real order flow; synthetic accuracy alone does not establish real-market robustness.
infographic.paper_title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books

title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology
authors: Imanol García de Beristain, David Nieto Simavilla, Marco Ellero
abstract: We present GINNGER (GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for GEnerative Rheology), a framework for discovering thermodynamically admissible constitutive equations from microstructural flow data. Unlike existing approaches that learn constitutive operators, GINNGER reformulates constitutive discovery as the learning of the underlying thermodynamic generators from which constitutive equations emerge. Embedding the GENERIC formalism into the learning process restricts the search to constitutive models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction, eliminating the need to prescribe phenomenological constitutive equations a priori. A second conceptual advance is a spectral formulation of constitutive discovery in the intrinsic eigenspace of the polymer conformation tensor. This provides a kinematics-independent thermodynamic state space in which the thermodynamic generators depend only on the instantaneous microstructural state, while flow kinematics acts solely as an external driver transporting the system through this space. Consequently, data from shear, extensional, and mixed flows contribute to the discovery of a single constitutive model that generalizes across deformation protocols and flow geometries. By learning thermodynamic generators rather than high-dimensional constitutive operators, GINNGER substantially reduces the complexity of the discovery problem while preserving thermodynamic consistency, material objectivity, and physical interpretability by construction. The framework is validated using high-fidelity simulations, accurately reconstructing constitutive behavior and predicting complex flow fields across previously unseen geometries. GINNGER establishes a new paradigm for constitutive discovery by combining generative, spectral, and thermodynamically grounded learning within a unified framework for data-driven modeling of complex fluids.

infographic.key_insight: GINNGER learns thermodynamic generators rather than constitutive operators, yielding rheological models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports physically consistent complex-fluid modeling across deformation protocols and flow geometries without prescribing phenomenological constitutive equations.
method: Embed the GENERIC formalism into neural-network learning of thermodynamic generators.
Represent microstructural states in the polymer conformation tensor’s intrinsic eigenspace.
Combine shear, extensional, and mixed-flow data to discover a unified constitutive model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation using high-fidelity simulations reports accurate constitutive reconstruction and complex-flow predictions in previously unseen geometries.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative error metrics or experimental validation, leaving real-material accuracy to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology

title: A Comprehensive Survey of Crystal Structural Prototypes: Construction, Classification, and Applications
authors: Jianjun Hu, Ying Feng, Rongzhi Dong, Jeffrey Hu, Remy Rogers, Dipannoy Gupta
abstract: Crystal structural prototypes describe recurring atomic arrangements across chemically distinct materials. Prototype libraries are built through crystallographic curation, standardization, geometric matching, local-environment clustering, and periodic-graph analysis, and support chemical substitution, derivative enumeration, high-throughput screening, structure solution, crystal structure prediction (CSP), and generative design. This survey compares methods by the structural information they retain and the equivalence rules they impose, distinguishing crystallographic structure types, geometric realizations, chemistry-anonymous topologies, and chemical decorations. We review curated and automatically extracted prototype libraries (AFLOW, CSPD, LAE-ICSPD, EMFDTW, TYPIX, ICSD structure types), their source databases, and algorithms for assigning family membership. A GraphID-based analysis of samples from ICSD, the Materials Project, OQMD, and LeMat shows that the 100 most frequent families in each sample cover 30 to 67 percent of analyzed structures, while 72 to 82 percent of observed families are singletons. The GraphIDs of up to 76 percent of structures change when the neighbor tolerance is varied. In our comparison of 12 generative CSP models, template retrieval achieves the highest top-1 success rate. Removing a reduced-stoichiometry class from training introduces new failures in 50 to 78 percent of the test structures of that class, which measures sensitivity to stoichiometric coverage, not generalization to unseen prototypes. We relate these findings to earlier statistics of structure types, space groups, and periodic nets, and to protein-fold coverage studies. We propose independent-database coverage measurements, discovery-rate analyses, and family-held-out tests to assess how prototype reuse affects prediction accuracy, generalization, and novelty.

infographic.key_insight: Crystal prototype reuse supports materials discovery, but measured family coverage and novelty depend strongly on structural equivalence rules.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Prototype libraries can accelerate substitution screening and crystal structure prediction, provided family definitions and training coverage are validated.
method: Compare prototype libraries, construction methods, and structural equivalence rules.
Analyze GraphID family distributions across ICSD, Materials Project, OQMD, and LeMat samples.
Compare 12 generative CSP models and test sensitivity to withheld stoichiometry classes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The top 100 families cover 30–67% of sampled structures, 72–82% of observed families are singletons, and template retrieval achieves the highest top-1 success rate in the model comparison.
infographic.watch_item: Up to 76% of structures change GraphID with neighbor tolerance; withholding stoichiometry classes does not establish generalization to unseen prototypes.
infographic.paper_title: A Comprehensive Survey of Crystal Structural Prototypes: Construction, Classification, and Applications

title: topas-editor and TOPilot: tools for AI-driven analysis of diffraction and total scattering data
authors: John S. O. Evans, Oliver J. Wagstaff, Ivana R. Evans, Arnt Kern, Alan A. Coelho
abstract: This paper describes topas-editor and TOPilot, which provide a powerful interface to the TOPAS software suite and allow generative AI-driven automation of complex crystallographic tasks. topas-editor is a TOPAS-aware VS Code extension designed for the rapid creation and editing of TOPAS input files and for interacting with the software. It knows TOPAS syntax, has crystallographic-aware editing features and provides in-line user guidance via hover tips and automated links to reference manuals. TOPilot is a collection of Python routines and machine-accessible reference documents that allow AI-driven automated analysis in TOPAS. It uses a transferable topas-inp-writer skill that can be applied in all TOPAS application areas. We demonstrate the power and reliability of the approach using examples including: a complex Rietveld refinement with sample- and data-related complications; automatic analysis of multiple data sets; a pipeline from indexing through structure solution to refinement; automatic identification of the phases present in a sample; single crystal and powder diffraction analysis of incommensurate structures; and fitting PDF data. TOPilot can be used directly alongside topas-editor, via a stand-alone topilot-wizard, or via command line interfaces or desktop apps from major AI providers. TOPilot was developed and tested using Claude large language models, but can be configured to use other cloud or local models. topas-editor and TOPilot are freely available.

infographic.key_insight: topas-editor and TOPilot connect generative AI with TOPAS to automate crystallographic analysis of diffraction and total scattering data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These freely available tools can streamline structure characterization workflows, from phase identification and structure solution to refinement and pair distribution function fitting.
method: Use a TOPAS-aware VS Code extension for input editing, syntax guidance and reference access.
Equip AI with Python routines, machine-accessible documentation and a transferable topas-inp-writer skill.
Run workflows through the editor, a standalone wizard, command-line interfaces or AI desktop apps.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations spanning complex Rietveld refinement, multiple-data-set analysis, indexing-to-refinement workflows, phase identification, incommensurate structures and PDF fitting, but provides no quantitative performance metrics.

infographic.paper_title: topas-editor and TOPilot: tools for AI-driven analysis of diffraction and total scattering data

title: pymatgen: 15 years of community growth, new functionality, and future prospects
authors: Janine George, Matthew K. Horton, Aaron D. Kaplan, Seán R. Kavanagh, Janosh Riebesell, Andrew S. Rosen
abstract: We present a retrospective on the Python Materials Genomics (pymatgen) library, reflecting on 15 years of community growth and established best practices. The current version of pymatgen builds on its robust, open-source foundation, emphasising its collaborative nature. Over the past decade, pymatgen has thrived as one of the largest open-source materials science codebases. We detail how pymatgen supports advanced computational materials science workflows, how it adapts to changing demands, and the lessons learned from its growing community, providing guidance beyond pymatgen's open-source community. Pymatgen will continue to evolve in response to the current rapidly changing landscape of computational materials science and materials informatics. We discuss the challenges and potential solutions to managing the community-driven evolution of pymatgen and provide an outlook on its future development.

infographic.key_insight: Pymatgen’s 15-year evolution shows how community-driven, open-source infrastructure can support changing computational materials science workflows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pymatgen provides a foundation for materials computation and informatics, while its development experience offers lessons for maintaining collaborative scientific software.
method: Review 15 years of community growth and established practices.
Describe support for advanced computational materials workflows.
Discuss development challenges, potential solutions, and future directions.

title: Material dependence of direct light-induced charge injection from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbates
authors: Jordan Alan Edwards, Johannes Lischner
abstract: Direct injection of charge from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbed molecules via the chemical interface damping of localized surface plasmons has emerged as a promising avenue to avoid the rapid thermalization of hot carriers. In this paper, we develop an approach for predicting hot-electron and hot-hole injection rates from large spherical nanoparticles into adsorbed carbon monoxide (CO) molecules. The approach combines a detailed description of the adsorbate-metal interactions via ab initio density functional theory with a macroscopic electrodynamics treatment of the localized surface plasmon. We apply this approach to nine different metals including both traditional (Ag, Au, Cu) and emerging (Al) plasmonic metals as well as non-plasmonic metals (Ni, Rh, Pd, Ir, Pt). For all metals, hot-electron injection is larger than hot-hole injection. This is a consequence of the alignment of the CO frontier orbitals, with the CO lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) being closer to the metal Fermi energy than the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO). The largest electron injection rates in the optical photon ranges are obtained for Al, Ag, Cu and Au, with Cu and Au showing significant plasmonic enhancement. The non-plasmonic metals show weak electron injection as a consequence of their high LUMO energies relative to the metal Fermi level. The results of our study pave the way towards a rational design of metallic nanoscale photocatalysts for specific chemical processes.

infographic.key_insight: Metal choice controls direct light-induced charge injection into adsorbed CO, with electron injection exceeding hole injection across all nine metals studied.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Selecting suitable metals and adsorbate energy-level alignment could guide nanoscale photocatalyst design while bypassing rapid hot-carrier thermalization.
method: Model CO–metal interactions using ab initio density functional theory.
Describe localized surface plasmons using macroscopic electrodynamics.
Predict electron and hole injection rates from large spherical nanoparticles.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nine metals, Al, Ag, Cu and Au yielded the largest electron injection rates at optical photon energies, with significant plasmonic enhancement for Cu and Au.
infographic.watch_item: The predictions concern CO on large spherical nanoparticles; applicability to other adsorbates or particle geometries requires further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Material dependence of direct light-induced charge injection from metallic nanoparticles into adsorbates

title: The effect of oxygen on the surface tension of AlTi metallic alloys
authors: Yuna Kato, Jürgen Brillo, Thomas Voigtmann, Linnea Heitmeier
abstract: We perform molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of AlTi metallic alloy melts, with a specific focus on surface properties and the effect of oxygen. The simulations use a machine-learned inter- action potential (MLIP) that has recently been tested through experimental data for the statical and dynamical properties of AlTi melts in the bulk [Kato et al. (2026)]. We find that the surface- tension response to oxygen depends strongly on the AlTi composition. Element-resolved density profiles show that oxygen enrichment near the interface is accompanied by a suppression of the Al surface segregation observed in the oxygen-free liquid. The results are compared to experimental values obtained using levitation techniques in microgravity.

infographic.key_insight: Oxygen changes AlTi melt surface tension in a composition-dependent way, while interfacial oxygen enrichment suppresses aluminum surface segregation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling oxygen and alloy composition may help tune interfacial behavior in molten AlTi processing.
method: Molecular dynamics simulations of AlTi melts with oxygen.
Machine-learned interatomic potential previously tested against bulk experimental data.
Element-resolved density profiles to assess surface segregation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulated surface-tension results are compared with microgravity levitation measurements, but the abstract reports no quantitative agreement metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Prior testing on bulk melts does not by itself establish the potential’s accuracy for oxygen-containing interfaces.
infographic.paper_title: The effect of oxygen on the surface tension of AlTi metallic alloys

title: Bond-informed search for ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys
authors: Gaurav Arora, Alex Tai, Rodrigo Freitas, David Cereceda
abstract: Ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) control their local structure and influence a broad range of mechanical and thermodynamic properties. Yet they are notoriously difficult to identify. Locating low-energy ordered candidates requires exploring a configurational space that grows combinatorially with the number of elements, and Monte Carlo searches driven by density-functional theory (DFT) need a new electronic-structure calculation at every trial step. Here we introduce MECx (Minimum Energy Configuration eXplorer), a framework that guides Monte Carlo searches with a surrogate energy model trained on configurations stratified in bond-count space. Applied to ternary, quaternary, and quinary BCC alloys using compact training sets of 100 DFT-labeled configurations, MECx identifies ordered configurations with lower energies than those found by direct DFT-based Monte Carlo within practical computational limits. These configurations exhibit distinct pair-specific ordering, including B2- and B32-like motifs, and undergo progressive disordering as temperature increases. The MPEA-trained models also transfer to selected binary subsystems without retraining. The resulting ordered configurations agree with those obtained by direct DFT-based Monte Carlo and produce experimentally distinguishable superlattice reflections in simulated neutron diffraction patterns.

infographic.key_insight: MECx uses a bond-informed surrogate energy model to find low-energy ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys more efficiently than direct DFT-driven Monte Carlo.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Identifying alloy ordering can help engineers understand local structures that influence mechanical and thermodynamic properties.
method: Select training configurations stratified in bond-count space.
Train surrogate energy models on 100 DFT-labeled configurations per alloy.
Guide Monte Carlo searches and examine ordering, thermal disordering, and diffraction signatures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on ternary, quaternary, and quinary BCC alloys found lower-energy candidates than direct DFT-based Monte Carlo within practical computational limits, with transfer to selected binary subsystems without retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability beyond the tested BCC alloys and selected binary subsystems remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Bond-informed search for ordered configurations in multi-principal element alloys

title: Confinement-induced toughening in delignified wood-polyacrylamide composite hydrogels
authors: Kohei Shimogata, Tetsuo Yamaguchi
abstract: With growing interest in environmental conservation, polymer composites incorporating wood-derived materials have attracted significant attention. While research has focused extensively on hard composites utilizing delignified wood or cellulose nanofibers (CNF) and soft composites reinforced with CNF, there have been a limited number of studies on the development of soft composites that utilize the porous cellular structure of wood, with few exceptions. In this study, we fabricated soft composites by infiltrating delignified wood with polyacrylamide hydrogel and subjected them to uniaxial compression tests. The results demonstrated that these materials exhibited far superior strength and toughness compared to either delignified wood or polyacrylamide hydrogel alone. Through systematic investigation and theoretical analysis, we identified the mechanisms underlying these enhancements in strength and toughness. Specifically, in addition to the sacrificial bond breakage known to enhance toughness in double-network hydrogels, we propose that mechanical confinement, arising from the soft, incompressible hydrogel filling the hollow cell lumens, generates excess stress and acts to resist compressive deformation. This approach, which utilizes the cellular structure as a filler, suggests the potential for creating a new class of high-toughness composite materials.

infographic.key_insight: Filling delignified wood’s cellular pores with polyacrylamide hydrogel enhances compressive strength and toughness through sacrificial bond breakage and proposed mechanical confinement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Wood’s porous architecture offers a route to tougher soft composites by constraining a nearly incompressible hydrogel within cell lumens.
method: Infiltrate delignified wood with polyacrylamide hydrogel.
Evaluate the composites using uniaxial compression tests.
Investigate toughening mechanisms through systematic experiments and theoretical analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Compression tests showed substantially greater strength and toughness than either constituent alone, although the abstract provides no numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: Performance under repeated loading and deformation modes beyond uniaxial compression remains unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Confinement-induced toughening in delignified wood-polyacrylamide composite hydrogels

title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Yutong Wu, Yi-Xin Liu
abstract: Advances in polymer synthesis and computational modeling are expanding the block-copolymer architecture space accessible for phase-behavior design. Machine learning can accelerate this exploration, yet a common representation capable of learning across diverse chain topologies remains lacking. Here, we present a graph neural network (GNN) representation of acyclic AB multiblock architectures, tested by random-phase approximation (RPA) instability prediction. Each chain is represented as a graph, enabling a common model to learn across diverse topologies. This representation, which organizes RPA-related information, retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks and demonstrates its potential for reuse across tasks through transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction. By effectively linking block-copolymer chain architecture to field-theoretic response, this graph representation not only reconstructs stability-limit curves but also provides a practical route for future self-consistent field theory exploration of ordered phase space across complex topologies.

infographic.key_insight: A graph neural representation links diverse acyclic AB block-copolymer architectures to RPA instability limits and generalizes to chains with more blocks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate architecture screening for polymer phase-behavior design and support future self-consistent field theory exploration.
method: Represent acyclic AB multiblock chains as graphs.
Train a common GNN to predict random-phase approximation instability limits across topologies.
Test extrapolation to more-block architectures and transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reconstruction of stability-limit curves, retained predictive capability on architectures with more blocks, and transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction, but gives no quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Validation targets RPA instability rather than ordered-phase prediction; applicability to cyclic chains and experimental phase behavior remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits

title: Temperature and Thickness Dependent Spin Current Transmission through Epitaxial Antiferromagnetic α-Fe2O3
authors: Koushik Prabhakara, Rajeev Nepal, Subhashree Chatterjee, Rabindra Basnet, Ezana Negusse, Ramesh C Budhani
abstract: Antiferromagnetic insulator α-Fe2O3 is a potential medium for coherent motion of spin waves over relatively large distances, allowing non-dissipative transfer of information between circuit elements. However, the structural defects and temperature dependent spin reorientations in this oxide impact the propagation. Understanding how the magnetic state of an antiferromagnetic insulator affects spin-current transmission is therefore important for elucidating the mechanisms governing spin transport. Here, we report spin-current transmission through epitaxial α-Fe2O3 thin films sandwiched between Permalloy and Pt. Using spin pumping and inverse spin Hall effect, we observe a finite symmetric dc voltage across the Pt layer over the temperature range 1.6 to 300 K for alpha-Fe2O3 thicknesses of 0, 30, 40, and 100 nm. The symmetric voltage coefficient Ks exhibits two approximately linear temperature regimes, separated by a characteristic temperature T* whose value depends on the thickness of the α-Fe2O3 layer. Further, the dc magnetization measurements on some of the samples suggest that the T* is correlated with the spin reorientation transition (Morin transition) in α-Fe2O3. Interestingly, a significantly larger magnitude of dKs/dT is noted below the characteristic temperature T*. The observed thickness and temperature dependent spin-current transmission indicates a sensitivity to the magnetic state of the insulating hematite layer.

infographic.key_insight: Spin-current transmission through epitaxial α-Fe2O3 depends on temperature and thickness, with a characteristic temperature linked to magnetic spin reorientation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hematite-based spintronic interconnects may require thickness control and operating-temperature selection to account for changes in spin-current transmission.
method: Sandwich epitaxial α-Fe2O3 films between Permalloy and Pt.
Probe spin transmission using spin pumping and the inverse spin Hall effect.
Compare temperature-dependent voltage responses with dc magnetization measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1.6–300 K and α-Fe2O3 thicknesses of 0, 30, 40, and 100 nm, a finite symmetric dc voltage was observed; its coefficient Ks showed two approximately linear temperature regimes with a larger slope magnitude below a thickness-dependent T*.
infographic.watch_item: The correlation between T* and the Morin transition is suggested by magnetization measurements on only some samples, rather than established across the full thickness series.
infographic.paper_title: Temperature and Thickness Dependent Spin Current Transmission through Epitaxial Antiferromagnetic α-Fe2O3

title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
authors: Kun Ryu, Yeo Jin Jung, Shyue Ping Ong, Claire Donnat, Ying Shirley Meng
abstract: Automated materials discovery requires evaluating large pools of candidate configurations, with density functional theory (DFT) as a major throughput bottleneck. Pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate DFT cheaply, but their errors vary by orders of magnitude across configurations, making it difficult to decide when to trust the MLIP predictions and when to fall back to DFT. We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $α$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $α=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP's latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

infographic.key_insight: A structure-only predictor with conformal risk control selects configurations for DFT while controlling the MLIP error retained on unselected configurations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Risk-controlled DFT routing can reduce expensive labeling in automated materials discovery without requiring access to MLIP internals.
method: Convert atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates into fixed geometric descriptors.
Predict MLIP–DFT disagreement in energy, average force, and maximum force.
Calibrate a DFT-selection threshold using conformal risk control and a user-chosen error fraction α.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight dataset–MLIP pairs under an identical guarantee, the predictor routed 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT than committee baselines at α = 0.3.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantee controls aggregate retained error, not every configuration’s accuracy; gains also narrow when DFT labeling settings match MLIP training settings.
infographic.paper_title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials

title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
authors: Seungone Kim, Jiayi Geng, Young-Jun Lee, Bo Liu, Juyoung Suk, Nicholas Lubbers
abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

infographic.key_insight: Across 135 AI-generated follow-up papers on open scientific problems, none met all scientist-defined conditions, despite producing plausible-looking research papers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineering teams should verify AI-generated research claims against recorded evidence before relying on them for materials or simulation decisions.
method: Provide agents with a science paper and an unpublished follow-up direction from a DOE national laboratory scientist.
Evaluate submissions using scientist-defined conditions and an integrity check.
Test nine frontier agents on 15 problems spanning five scientific domains.
infographic.evidence_signal: None of the 135 submissions satisfied all conditions, and 114 failed integrity checks, most often for claiming unperformed work or reporting numbers inconsistent with recorded evidence.
infographic.watch_item: The benchmark spans multiple fields; the abstract does not report materials-science-specific performance.
infographic.paper_title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
